## Architecture

**Rust decides, AVFoundation and Metal do** (spec §7). The core holds the
project (JSON, spec §5.2), every edit, the composition plan, the per-frame
recipe, the index of a WebM/Matroska file being imported and the WebM file an
`av1_webm`, `vp9_webm` or `vp9_alpha_webm` export writes (its container only; the packets come from Swift). Swift owns windows, gestures, undo, AVFoundation playback and export,
the Metal compositor, media import and its caches and on-device analysis of
the media (Vision and Sound Analysis on the analysis lane, cached per media
in `cache/analysis/`; the core reads only what a tool or op hands it), and
agent dispatch. No
pixel or sample work in Rust; no ffmpeg dependency in the product. The AV1 and
VP9 encoders (SVT-AV1, libvpx; `designs/adr/codec-export.md`) are
platform-side like AVFoundation: Swift calls them through the bridging header,
no `rc_*` export wraps them (spec §11 CX-4).

### FFI contract

- `core/include/framejob_core.h` is a **hand-maintained** C header, the single
  contract between the worlds. **The FFI is three files in lockstep**: a Rust
  `#[no_mangle]` export, its entry in the header, and its wrapper in
  `app/Sources/ReelCore.swift` and its `ReelCore+<Area>.swift` files, **the
  only files that call `rc_*`** (spec §11 CJ-8 (l)); a new wrapper goes in
  the file of its area.
- A handle is an immutable project. **Every edit is pure and answers one of
  three arms** (`core/src/outcome.rs`, spec §5.5): applied with the new
  project, an identity, or refused in the rule's own sentence. Only the first
  is an undo step. `ProjectDocument` is the single mutation point and undo is
  its stack of handles.
- Edits are JSON ops through `rc_project_apply`. **The op table is two
  halves**: what an op MEANS is the module doc of `core/src/edit.rs`, and
  what it TAKES — every argument's name, kind and required-ness — is
  `core/src/op_table.rs`, as data, published as JSON Schema by
  `rc_op_schemas`. `ReelOps.swift`'s typed builders,
  `AgentCatalog*.swift`'s tools and spec §6 mirror them — change one, change
  all four — **except that every op TOOL prints the arguments half instead of
  restating it** (`AgentCatalog.opTool`), so an argument added to an op costs
  a sentence of prose there and no schema. A tool that takes more or less
  than its op does says so in `AgentCatalog+Declarations.swift`, one row and
  one reason each. The envelope's `scope` key addresses an edit inside a
  nest.
- Persisted-state changes bump `RC_FORMAT_VERSION` in `core/src/format.rs`
  **and** the header.
- Errors: `rc_project_apply` returns NULL three distinguishable ways, and the
  two message channels are never both written. NULL with NEITHER written is
  an identity; NULL with `reason_out` set is a refusal and that string is the
  rule's own sentence; NULL with `err_out` set is invalid input. The first two
  make no undo step and only the third is an error. `"internal error: …"` is a
  caught panic.

### Where a feature lands — the standard recipe

Every shipped feature follows the same shape; putting a step's code anywhere
else is what bloats files:

1. **Core:** the op's semantics in an `impl Project` block in the module of
   its own concern (a new concern is a new module); the row in `edit.rs`'s
   enum and module-doc table, and its arguments in `op_table.rs` (which is
   where `OP_NAMES` comes from); a persisted field with a serde default and a
   `schema_vN.rs`; a new `core/tests/*.rs`. A field lands in the same phase as
   the thing that renders it.
2. **FFI**, only when a new `rc_*` export is needed: Rust → header →
   the ReelCore file of its area.
3. **Swift:** the typed builder in `ReelOps.swift`; a small value or model
   file; an `EditorViewController+<Feature>.swift` with its validator arm; an
   inspector section REGISTERED in `ClipPane.makeSections()`; a menu item in
   `AppDelegate+Menus.swift`; a gesture as a session struct.
4. **MCP mirror:** a handler in `AgentServer+<Feature>.swift`, a catalog entry
   declaring `scope`, and a comment naming the UI path it mirrors.
5. **Documents:** spec §5.2 / §6 / §7.10 for anything they mirror; the map
   entry in the per-side `CLAUDE.md` if a file's role changed; the feature's
   page in `docs/guide/` (and its README highlight and
   `menus-and-shortcuts.md` row when it adds one); the phase's record in its
   road map.
6. **Verify:** as "Verification" below says; then read the change back
   adversarially before committing.

## Rules

- Conventions are Rasterize's — `~/devel/rasterize`'s three `CLAUDE.md`
  files are the parent text for anything not settled here.
- **Every user-visible edit gets an MCP mirror** (spec §7.9): a handler, a
  catalog entry, and a comment naming the UI path. The startup parity check
  in `AgentServer.prepareCatalog()` has SIX parts: catalog names against handler
  names, every op in the core's table against the tools (through
  `rc_op_names`, with an explicit allow-list for ops that deliberately have
  none), each tool's schema shape, that every op tool declares `scope`,
  that every op tool declares the CORE's own arguments for its op — each one
  described, and no description for an argument no op has
  (`AgentServer+Parity.swift`), and that every tool `ModelKeys.keyed` names
  exists and its description carries its key's clause
  (`AgentServer+Parity.swift`, spec §11 CJ-13). What it cannot see is a CALL, which two
  things guard at dispatch: the argument GATE in `AgentServer+Gate.swift`
  compares the caller's keys to the schema the tool published and refuses a
  stranger by name, for all one hundred and twenty-five product tools (and the dev tools,
  road map 11), before any handler runs;
  and the throwing helpers in `AgentServer+Arguments.swift` refuse a value a
  handler cannot read by name rather than dropping it.
- **A feature that needs a language or cloud model tests its key through
  `ModelKeys`** (spec §11 CJ-3): presence, the sentence, the control's or
  menu item's mark, the tool's refusal where it would send, and a row in
  `ModelKeys.keyed`.
- **A file at the ~600-line cap gives something up before it takes anything
  on**, as a pure move landed and gated alone; new files are capped at 400
  lines. Frozen files take wiring only. `core/src/edit.rs` and
  `app/Sources/ReelOps.swift` are exempt (tables, one row per op), and proof
  instruments in `tools/proof/` are held to neither cap. The ledger is
  `wc -l app/Sources/*.swift core/src/*.rs graphic/src/*.rs | sort -rn`; the
  seam a record already named for a file is under "Named next cuts" in
  `designs/adr/app-file-history.md` / `core-file-history.md`.
- **Size rules are per FILE, never per feature.** A brief, design, road map,
  spec or proof never sets a budget on how many lines a feature may add,
  never measures a feature's total against one, and never names code size as
  a reason to cut, trim or drop a feature: a feature takes as much code as it
  needs. Keeping files small is the cap above and its pure moves, nothing
  else (owner, 2026-10-10).
- **A decision in spec §11 is not re-litigated** (`designs/spec/11-decisions/`). A phase that needs a new
  one records it there before the code, not after.
- **`.secrets/` (gitignored) holds the owner's own keys for proofs**, e.g.
  `.secrets/anthropic-key`, read ONLY by `anthropic_key()` in
  `tools/proof/assistant_prompt_eval.py`. Never open, print, grep, copy or
  list its contents; never move a key from it into an argument, the
  environment of a build, a log or a file. A run that spends money still
  needs its explicit flags (`--live --cap <dollars>`); the file's presence
  spends nothing. Every paid proof request is also held to the month's
  budget (spec §11 P-3, P-6) in
  `~/Library/Application Support/Frame Job Proofs/spend.jsonl`; an agent
  never edits it, raises a budget, or points a verification at it.
- **A check only a person at the machine can make is a row in
  `docs/manual-checks.md`**, added in the change that creates it — never a
  `ready-for-human` issue, and never an instrument built to stand in for the
  person (how a pane looks, whether audio plays, a real key's conversation).
  Automate what a script can truly measure; list only the residue.
- Commit only when asked. A commit message says what was verified and what
  is owed, and the road map's record says the same.

## Verifying a build

A local Distribution build is only ever checked, never launched: it loads
Sparkle, which library validation refuses in an ad-hoc signed hardened app
(spec §11 PUB-7). Debug and Release link with `-dead_strip_dylibs`, so they
never load it.

The app is verified by driving the built binary over MCP and comparing what
it renders — not by reading code. Launch your own instance on your own socket
and only ever kill that one (`pgrep -f "MacOS/Frame Job"` lists them, Debug
and Release alike; the products folder tells them apart; another session may
have one running):

```sh
make app-debug
python3 tools/proof/proof_app.py launch   # prints folder, socket, log, pid
```

Each later command names the printed folder literally
(`mcp.MCP("<dir>/agent.sock")`, `python3 tools/proof/phaseN_proof.py
<dir>/agent.sock`, `grep "Frame Job: " <dir>/framejob.log`), because a shell
variable does not survive from one agent command to the next; stop it by the
pid the launcher prints.

The log line `Frame Job agent socket listening at <dir>/agent.sock` says it is
up (`not bound: <reason>` says why not). Drive it with `tools/proof/mcp.py`'s
`mcp.MCP("<dir>/agent.sock")` (streamable HTTP over the Unix socket), or with
the bundled stdio helper `framejob-mcp` with `RC_AGENT_SOCKET` set to the same
path: one tool per §6 op, each taking the `scope`
envelope key, plus the app-state tools — `open_project`, `new_project`,
`new_project_from_range`, `save_project`, `close_project`, `get_project`, `import_media`,
`import_captions`, `export_captions`, `transcribe`, `consolidate_media`, `detect_silence`,
`detect_fillers`, `transcribe_for_fillers`, `get_transcript`, `get_timeline_transcript`, `get_media_analysis`, `split_at_shots`, `normalize_clip`, `enhance_voice`, `match_audio`, `set_playhead`, `set_range`, `set_selection`, `set_scope`,
`undo`, `redo`, `render_frame`, `export`, `export_status`, `auto_zoom`, `add_shortcut_overlays`, `speed_up_typing`, `cancel_export`,
`record_screen`, `write_graphic`,
`get_graphic`, `graphic_reference`, `render_graphic`, `import_graphic_font`,
`import_graphic_asset`, `delete_graphic`, `rename_graphic`,
`restore_graphic`, `list_graphics`, `insert_graphic`, `export_graphic` and `import_graphic`. A Debug or Release build also has the dev tools
(`snapshot_ui`, `perform_menu_item`, `cancel_sheet`, `select_inspector_tab`;
"Seeing the chrome" below; `play_preview`, which plays a window's preview
for a while and answers the frames composed (#127, spec §11 G-36);
`graphic_memory`, which answers the graphic rasters' memory budget, what is
held and kept, and simulates memory pressure (G-37); `loudness_meter`, which
answers a window's live loudness meter (momentary, short-term, integrated,
true peak, the frames measured and its resets) and resets it (road map
"audio" AP7, AU-77); `land_recording`, which lands fixture files as a
finished recording through the recorder panel's door or `record_screen`'s,
so a proof can watch Enhance the microphone when it lands without a
microphone grant (spec §11 AU-69); and
`analysis_job`, which wants a media's analysis under a document's stand-in
owner and returns at once, or waits for every such job and answers their
runs (spec §11 CJ-27); and `-RCDevAnalysisHold <s>`, which holds each
analysis job before its first frame, polling cancellation, so a proof can
act during it; and `-RCDevAnalysisCanned YES`, with which a canned analysis
marker is honoured (spec §11 CJ-26); and `transcript_view`, which answers
what a window's Transcript tab shows — its tokens, paragraphs, highlight,
selection, fill and status — after focusing its view, selecting words or
clicking one (road map "creator-jobs" TX2a, spec §11 TX-23); and
`playback_rebuilds`, which answers a window's preview rebuilds since the last
reset, each with the milliseconds to its build and to its landing (road map
"creator-jobs" SW0, spec §11 SW-1), with the dev-only launch default
`-RCDevRebuildHold <s>`, which holds each rebuild's landing so a proof can
make two edits inside one flight (SW-4); and
`assistant_send` / `assistant_answer`, which
drive a window's assistant turn against a stand-in server, with the dev-only
launch default `-RCDevAssistantSend <text> -RCDevAssistantReport <path>` for
a turn in a launch without the server; and `-RCDevSyncHold <s>`, which holds
Synchronize Audio's background analysis so a proof can act during it; and
`-RCDevRampRenderHold <s>`, which holds each speed-ramp audio render so a
proof can act while it is pending; and `-RCDevCursorLoadHold <s>`, which
holds each cursor track's load so a proof can act while it is pending (road
map creator-jobs CU2, spec §11 CU-26); and `-RCDevWebMFault audio@N|video@N|audio-hold@N`,
which puts a fault in an `av1_webm` export's audio pump or video sink so a
proof can time the stop, spec §11 CX-15 (6); and

its own Import so a proof can see a package land (spec §11 G-47); and

and the catalog are the authority for the counts; the parity check compares

puts the job on the Export Queue and answers an `export_id` at once, and
`export_status` answers it until `done` (`mcp.py`'s `export_with` waits; spec
§11 #326).

A proof picks its app through `tools/proof/proof_app.py`: `RC_PROOF_APP` is
`debug` (the default), `release` or a `.app` path. `mcp.launch`, `mcp.MCP` and
`python3 tools/proof/proof_app.py launch` refuse a tree's built app when any
input is newer than its last complete build (its
`_CodeSignature/CodeResources`), or an instance started before an input
changed, naming the file, its time and the `make` target.

Release-only proofs pass `release_only=` (`git grep release_only= tools/proof`);
recording_proof's socket instance is started with
`python3 tools/proof/proof_app.py launch --app release`.

**Before trusting any MCP proof, `grep "Frame Job: " <dir>/framejob.log`
must print nothing** — that prefix is the startup parity check complaining.
On a Debug build the same complaint is an `assertionFailure` that traps first
(`AgentServer.prepareCatalog`), so `make app-debug` fails at Write Agent
Catalog with `Fatal error: …` instead of logging the line.

A proof's instance shares its bundle's defaults domain (the owner's
`com.kgalligan.FrameJob` for a Release build, `com.kgalligan.FrameJob.debug`
for a Debug build, spec §11 V-5): no
environment moves `UserDefaults` (#238). Never perform a persisting menu item
(View ▸ Snapping, Safe Areas, Hide Inspector, Timeline Track Height, Preview
Quality) on either build: `mcp.py` ends the script with status 3 and
`DEFAULTS MOVED` last on stderr when its session moved a key and no other
Frame Job shares the domain, and only prints the line when one does;
`defaults_proof.py` is its proof. The guard reads the domain with
`CFFIXED_USER_HOME` taken out of `defaults`' environment
(`proof_defaults.read_env`), so a proof run under a scratch home that does
not exist yet, or is removed before the script ends, is compared with
itself: `defaults export` answers no key under a variable naming an absent
folder.

**`tools/proof/` holds the scripts that do this** — an MCP script per phase
over a dependency-free client (`mcp.py`), and beside most of them an
offscreen-chrome script or a probe. Every claim in them is a placement read
back through `get_project`, a BYTE comparison of two PNGs, or a
sample-for-sample comparison of two exports decoded to PCM (which needs
`ffmpeg` at proof time). Its README says how to make the test media, run
one, and which scores are known host-state skips (a locked console, a
Bluetooth output). Add the next phase's proof there rather than writing a
throwaway. An instance DEADLOCKS somewhere past forty documents open at once:
a proof that closes what it opens (`close_project`) can share an instance, and
one that does not relaunches between proof sessions.

Spec §10's per-step verifications are the acceptance tests. What no script
can answer — step 4's "the clip plays with audio", step 5's 60 fps, and the
rest — is a row in `docs/manual-checks.md`, which the owner runs.

## Verification

- **In the loop:** a targeted test (`cd core && cargo test --release --test
  <file> <filter>`), `make lint` after Rust edits, `make typecheck` after Swift
  edits, `make app-debug` before driving the app, and the phase's own rows
  (`--only` where the proof has it) against Debug.
- **Once, when the code is complete:** `make gate`, in the foreground, under
  the 600 s tool cap (`make gate GATE_ARGS=--force` only when a stamp itself is
  in doubt). It stops at the first failure and skips a step whose inputs and
  tools are byte-identical to its last pass, so after a fix it re-runs only
  what the fix can change. Never run one of its steps by hand to stand in for
  it, never re-run an unchanged step, and never run anything twice with no
  edit between.
- **The proof a phase records** runs whole once, on the final instrument,
  against Release (`RC_PROOF_APP=release` after the gate's `make app`), with
  any `release_only` proof the change touches. This is a rule: nothing checks
  which build a recorded run drove.
- **A proof that fails only on Debug** is pinned `release_only="<reason>"` in
  the change that finds it (spec §11 V-4); an assert trap on Debug is a defect
  to fix, never a pin.
- **Mutants** target the decisions the phase adds: about one per new branch,
  threshold, refusal or ordering, usually 3–8; more than 10 only with a reason
  written in the spec. The full set runs once, at the end, on the final
  instrument.
- **A fix pass** re-runs only the rows whose instrument code it changed and
  the mutants whose anchor lines it touched, then `make gate`.
- **Background** only for a command that cannot fit 600 s, waited on once with
  a bound; never a poll loop.

## Seeing the chrome

`screencapture` needs a Screen Recording grant the agent's terminal may or
may not have (it varies by host and session), and without it `screencapture`
silently writes a black PNG. Assume neither: a proof that needs the grant
probes for it and skips its granted tier by name, and a capture is never
trusted until it is checked non-black. The way to LOOK at the chrome is
**`tools/proof/harness/`**: it compiles every file in `app/Sources` except
`main.swift` with a `main.swift` of its own, links the staticlib, opens a
`.framejob` package, puts an `EditorViewController` in an `NSWindow` and
`cacheDisplay`s it into a PNG at the display's backing scale — the same paint
path the window uses, no TCC grant, either appearance, captured on SETTLE.
The preview well comes out as the canvas background (an `AVPlayerLayer` or
Metal layer does not draw into `cacheDisplay`), so nothing about the PICTURE
is ever claimed offscreen; pixel claims go over MCP. `tools/proof/README.md`'s
"offscreen harness" section has the build line, the argument list and the
pinned `UserDefaults`.

To look at the LIVE app, a Debug or Release build (`make app-debug`,
`make app`; never Distribution) has dev tools over MCP (road map 11, spec §11 V-1).
`snapshot_ui` captures the editor, a sheet, Settings, Welcome or the recorder panel, with a
layout dump. `perform_menu_item` runs a menu item by path to put a sheet or
Settings up, `cancel_sheet` closes the sheet, and `select_inspector_tab`
picks an inspector tab and sub-tab. All four work with the
app inactive and its window covered. A capture's look is set at launch with
the dev-only `-RCDevAppearance light|dark`, never switched live. To see every
catalogued screen at once, `python3 tools/proof/screens.py` walks
`designs/screens/`, once per look, each time on its own pinned instance. It
writes each screen's PNGs and layout dumps and one `screens.md` with the
prose and each capture's layout problems. The last screen is the recorder
panel: shown from the background it no longer takes key (#137), but an
instance that is active when it runs still gets a key panel with Record on
Return, so the script stops each instance straight after capturing it.

Two rules from it worth carrying into any proof: **identical, stable,
DIFFERENT output across processes is an Auto Layout ambiguity to find, not a
race to out-wait** — reach for constraint priorities, not for more run-loop
turns (on an `NSStackView` that is `setHuggingPriority(_:for:)`;
`setContentHuggingPriority` is inert on a stack); and **when the thing to
check is app ARITHMETIC or app STRUCTURE with
no caller a script can reach** (a menu, a validator, a cue builder, a queue),
the answer is a probe compiled from `app/Sources` through
`tools/proof/swift_build.py`, not a photograph. A probe that will not build is a scored
FAILURE, never an exit, so a rotted instrument cannot take a score down with
it. **That rule applies to historical instruments too.** The meter and welcome
comparisons build old `app/Sources` with the matching old core and header in
isolated output directories, using the current guarded `harness/main.swift`
for both paints; `cloud_captions_probe.py`'s W and SP baselines build the
same way through `reference_build.py`, each in its own folder. A failed current or reference build is a scored failure,
including an FFI diagnostic; it is never a historical skip or a reason to
fall back to the old harness. Only the recording proof's granted tier can
skip rows for a named host condition such as a locked console.

1	---
2	title: Remove Silences
3	description: Find the dead air in a spoken recording, see it on the timeline, and cut it all as one edit.
4	---
5	
6	import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
7	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
8	import Shot from '@components/Shot.astro';
9	
10	Remove Silences finds the dead air in a spoken recording, shows you what it would cut, and takes it all out as one undo step, closing the timeline over each cut. Use it on a screencast, a tutorial or a talking-head take.
11	
12	<AtAGlance
13	  menu="Clip ▸ Remove Silences…"
14	  tools={['detect_silence', 'ripple_delete_ranges']}
15	  needs="Nothing. Voice detection runs on your Mac, with no key and no upload."
16	/>
17	
18	## Remove the silences
19	
20	<Steps>
21	
22	1. To measure only some clips, select them first. The sheet then opens on **Selected clips**.
23	
24	2. Choose **Clip ▸ Remove Silences…**. It's available when the timeline has a clip with its sound on. If there turns out to be nothing to measure, Frame Job beeps instead of opening the sheet.
25	
26	3. Check what's shaded on the timeline, and read the count in the sheet, for example "23 cuts · removes 00:00:04:12". Both update as you change a control. With nothing to cut the count reads "No cuts" and **Remove** is dimmed.
27	
28	4. Adjust the [controls](#the-controls) until the cuts look right.
29	
30	5. Choose **Remove**. Everything shaded is cut and the timeline closes up. <kbd>⌘Z</kbd> puts it all back. Choose **Cancel** to leave the timeline as it was.
31	
32	</Steps>
33	
34	<Shot
35	  name="14-remove-silences-sheet.sheet"
36	  alt="The Remove Silences sheet, with Judge by set to Voice, a Level if no voice slider at −40 dBFS, Longer than 0.5 seconds, Keep at ends 0.1 seconds, and In set to All audible clips."
37	/>
38	
39	The sheet opens on its defaults every time. It doesn't remember your last settings.
40	
41	## The controls
42	
43	| Control | What it does | Default | Range |
44	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
45	| **Judge by:** | How a moment is tested. See [What counts as silent](/cleanup/voice-or-level/). | Voice, or Level if the voice model can't be used | Voice, Level |
46	| **Quieter than:** or **Level if no voice:** | The level that counts as quiet. The row reads **Quieter than:** in Level mode and **Level if no voice:** in Voice mode. | −40 dBFS | −80 to −10 dBFS |
47	| **Longer than:** | The shortest quiet stretch worth cutting. Shorter pauses, such as the gap between two words, stay. | 0.5 s | 0.05 to 10 s |
48	| **Keep at ends:** | How much of each quiet stretch to keep at each end, so speech doesn't start or stop abruptly. | 0.1 s | 0 to 2 s |
49	| **In:** | Whether to look at **Selected clips** or **All audible clips**. | Selected clips when the selection has something audible, otherwise All audible clips | |
50	
51	The level row is a slider in whole decibels, with its value beside it. In Level mode, sound at or below it is quiet. In Voice mode, it judges clips that hold no voice, and a clip the mix turns down to it or lower is quiet whatever it contains.
52	
53	**Selected clips** is greyed out when nothing selected makes a sound, and a selection of muted clips counts as nothing audible, as does a selected nest. Choose it to stop a music bed under a voice-over from holding the cuts up.
54	
55	**Longer than:** measures the stretch as you hear it, before **Keep at ends:** takes its share. A stretch no longer than twice **Keep at ends:** isn't cut. Cuts then [round to whole frames](/cleanup/how-cleanup-cuts-work/#frame-accurate-edges), so up to a frame more of room tone can remain at each end. Raise **Keep at ends:** if a word gets clipped.
56	
57	The two number fields take up to two decimal places. A number outside the range stays in the field and **Remove** beeps until you fix it. The count and the shading follow the slider as it moves, and a number field when you leave it.
58	
59	## What the sheet tells you
60	
61	The sheet explains itself under the count. It can show more than one of these at once.
62	
63	| The sheet says | What it means |
64	| --- | --- |
65	| "Nothing in this timeline is audible, so nothing was analysed." | Nothing the sheet is measuring makes a sound. With **Selected clips** it reads "Nothing the selected clips play is audible in the mix, so nothing was analysed." |
66	| "The waveform is still being analysed for …" or "Speech is still being analysed for …" | Frame Job hasn't finished with the files it names, which often happens straight after an import. Leave the sheet open and it updates as each one finishes. |
67	| "Nothing inside is proposed for removal yet." | Follows the line above: nothing in those files can be cut until their analysis is ready. |
68	| "Anything inside it that holds no voice is left alone until it lands…" | Follows the waveform line in Voice mode: speech can already be judged, but a clip with no voice has to wait for the waveform. It may add that the mix already turns a clip down far enough to be quiet. |
69	| "What is proposed inside … is quiet in the MIX…" | The named clips are still waiting for analysis, but they've been turned down, faded or ducked far enough to be quiet, so those cuts stand whatever the analysis finds. |
70	| "Quiet inside a nest is left alone…" | A quiet stretch at least as long as **Longer than:** ran across a nest. There may be dead air inside it, so a low count doesn't mean there's none. Open the nest with <kbd>⌘↓</kbd> and remove its silences there. With several nests it reads "Quiet inside 2 nests…". |
71	
72	Relinking a file starts its analysis again. If an agent relinks one while the sheet is open, the sheet clears the old results at once and updates when the new ones are ready.
73	
74	## Good to know
75	
76	- A gap with nothing audible in it is left alone, and so is a stretch where only a muted clip plays. Remove Silences takes dead air out of a recording, not the gaps you placed between clips. [Close Gap](/editing/close-gaps/) does that.
77	- With **Selected clips**, a moment none of those clips covers is never cut.
78	- The cut reaches every unlocked track, not only the clips you measured, and markers stay where they are. See [A ripple across every unlocked track](/cleanup/how-cleanup-cuts-work/#a-ripple-across-every-unlocked-track).
79	- Nothing inside a [nest](/editing/nests/) is cut, because a nest plays from its first frame and a cut into one would strand the rest of it. [Transitions are protected](/cleanup/how-cleanup-cuts-work/#transitions-are-protected) too.
80	- A quiet stretch broken up by a nest or a transition is measured in its pieces.
81	
82	## With an agent
83	
84	`detect_silence` reads the same ranges the sheet would cut and changes nothing. Pass them to `ripple_delete_ranges` to make the cut. See [Tools: clean-up](/mcp/tools-clean-up/).
85	
86	An agent isn't held to the limits of the sheet's controls, and it can also set how sure the voice model must be, which the sheet doesn't offer. To look inside a nest, it opens the nest with `set_scope` and reads again.
87	
88	## Related
89	
90	- [What counts as silent](/cleanup/voice-or-level/)
91	- [How a clean-up cut works](/cleanup/how-cleanup-cuts-work/)
92	- [Remove Filler Words](/cleanup/remove-filler-words/)
93	- [Close gaps and insert time](/editing/close-gaps/)
94	- [Work inside a nest](/editing/inside-a-nest/)

# CLAUDE.md — the documentation site

The public user documentation: Astro with Starlight, one page per feature or tight family of
features. `pnpm` manages it, and `engines` in `package.json` sets the Node it needs. `README.md` has
the commands.

## Where things are

```
astro.config.mjs        Starlight's settings: title, logo, fonts, theme, plugins
sidebar.mjs             every page's place in the navigation, in order
src/content/docs/       the pages: <section>/<page>.mdx
src/data/features.json  THE FEATURE LIST: what /features/ renders and what the proof reads
src/components/         AtAGlance (a page's facts), Shot (a screen in both looks),
                        FeatureIndex (the filterable list)
src/assets/screens/     WebP captures, written only by scripts/import-screens.mjs
src/styles/             the brand: the mark's inks, the app's faces, square chrome
```

## The rule that matters

**Every claim is written from the code.** A label, a default, a range, a shortcut, a limit or a
refusal is checked against `app/Sources/`, `core/src/`, `graphic/` or `mcp-proxy/` before it is
written, and the code wins over `docs/guide/`, a spec or an ADR. Never write what a feature
probably does. If the code cannot settle it, leave it out.

Nothing dev-only, deferred or unbuilt is documented. That excludes the dev tools (`snapshot_ui`,
`perform_menu_item`, `cancel_sheet`, `select_inspector_tab`, `play_preview`, `graphic_memory`,
`loudness_meter`, `land_recording`, `analysis_job`, `transcript_view`, `playback_rebuilds`,
`assistant_send`, `assistant_answer`) and every `-RCDev` launch default.

## Who reads this

Someone editing a video, who has never read this repository. They want to know what a thing does,
how to do it, and what will stop them. They do not care how it is built.

So a page never mentions: spec or decision IDs (`AU-12`, `§11`), road maps, phases, issue numbers,
source file or type names, `rc_*` exports, format version numbers, proofs, tests, or the history
...

Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. ## blender
You have access to Blender tools to interact with a Blender scene directly.
Blender must be running with the MCP add-on enabled and connected.

IMPORTANT: Respect existing structure and naming conventions.
NEVER assume missing values - inspect the scene first.
Do not destructively modify objects without confirmation.

# Bundled Manuals

Reference documentation is bundled alongside this server as plain-text RST files.
Search and read them directly with standard text tools (grep, file read, etc.):
  * `data/api/` - Blender Python API reference (RST files per module/class).
    Consult when writing or debugging `bpy` code: operator signatures, type
    properties, enum values, etc.
  * `data/manual/` - Blender user manual (RST files mirroring the official manual structure).
    Consult for conceptual explanations, workflow guidance, and feature overviews.

# Executing Code

The `execute_blender_code` tool runs Python code via `bpy` in the connected Blender instance.

The `execute_blender_code` tool is a last resort, if there are other tools that provide
the functionality you need, use those instead.

Prefer operators (`bpy.ops`) for standard actions (adding primitives, applying modifiers,
setting origins) - they handle defaults and context. Use the data API (`bpy.data`) for
precise control or to avoid side effects.

Many operators depend on the current mode (Object, Edit, Sculpt, etc.) and which objects
are active/selected. Verify or set the mode first - wrong mode either fails or silently
does nothing.

The **active object** and **selection** are distinct. Many operators require both.
Set them explicitly - do not assume the current state. Operators change selection and
active state as a side effect, so re-set both between sequential operator calls on
different objects.

Update the dependency graph after changes before reading computed properties
(world matrices, modifier results, etc.).

In edit mode, access mesh geometry through the bmesh API, not the regular mesh data API.
Flush bmesh changes back to the mesh - forgetting this silently loses all edits.

Return structured data (dicts, lists) from executed code, not print output.

# Scene & Data Structure

Blender uses a datablock system - objects and their underlying data (meshes, materials,
cameras, etc.) are separate entities.

Hierarchy:
  * **Scene** - top-level container. A .blend can have multiple.
  * **View Layer** - controls collection visibility/selectability.
  * **Collection** - organizational tree. Objects live in collections; can be nested;
    objects can belong to multiple collections.
  * **Object** - has a transform (location, rotation, scale) and references underlying data

1	# CLAUDE.md — the documentation site
2	
3	The public user documentation: Astro with Starlight, one page per feature or tight family of
4	features. `pnpm` manages it, and `engines` in `package.json` sets the Node it needs. `README.md` has
5	the commands.
6	
7	## Where things are
8	
9	```
10	astro.config.mjs        Starlight's settings: title, logo, fonts, theme, plugins
11	sidebar.mjs             every page's place in the navigation, in order
12	src/content/docs/       the pages: <section>/<page>.mdx
13	src/data/features.json  THE FEATURE LIST: what /features/ renders and what the proof reads
14	src/components/         AtAGlance (a page's facts), Shot (a screen in both looks),
15	                        FeatureIndex (the filterable list)
16	src/assets/screens/     WebP captures, written only by scripts/import-screens.mjs
17	src/styles/             the brand: the mark's inks, the app's faces, square chrome
18	```
19	
20	## The rule that matters
21	
22	**Every claim is written from the code.** A label, a default, a range, a shortcut, a limit or a
23	refusal is checked against `app/Sources/`, `core/src/`, `graphic/` or `mcp-proxy/` before it is
24	written, and the code wins over `docs/guide/`, a spec or an ADR. Never write what a feature
25	probably does. If the code cannot settle it, leave it out.
26	
27	Nothing dev-only, deferred or unbuilt is documented. That excludes the dev tools (`snapshot_ui`,
28	`perform_menu_item`, `cancel_sheet`, `select_inspector_tab`, `play_preview`, `graphic_memory`,
29	`loudness_meter`, `land_recording`, `analysis_job`, `transcript_view`, `playback_rebuilds`,
30	`assistant_send`, `assistant_answer`) and every `-RCDev` launch default.
31	
32	## Who reads this
33	
34	Someone editing a video, who has never read this repository. They want to know what a thing does,
35	how to do it, and what will stop them. They do not care how it is built.
36	
37	So a page never mentions: spec or decision IDs (`AU-12`, `§11`), road maps, phases, issue numbers,
38	source file or type names, `rc_*` exports, format version numbers, proofs, tests, or the history
39	of a feature. Internal words get translated: "refused" becomes what the user sees ("Frame Job
40	won't do this while…"), "the core" and "the op" disappear. A tool name is the one exception: the
41	MCP pages and `tools=` in `AtAGlance` name agent tools, because those are the product's interface.
42	
43	## Voice
44	
45	- Plain, direct and second person. Say what it does, then how. Short sentences.
46	- Open with what the feature is for, in a sentence or two, before any steps.
47	- British spelling in prose, as `docs/guide/` does (colour, centre, grey, normalise), and the
48	  app's exact spelling for its own labels (the **Color** tab, **Normalize**).
49	- Contractions are fine. No marketing: never "powerful", "seamless", "effortless", "robust",
50	  "simply", "just", "easily", "unleash", "supercharge".
51	- Prefer a full stop or a comma to an em dash.
52	- State defaults, ranges and limits as numbers. Say what happens at the edges, because that is
53	  what a reader comes to a reference for.
54	- No filler sections. A page with nothing to say under a heading doesn't have that heading.
55	
56	## Page shape
57	
58	```mdx
59	---
60	title: Markers
61	description: One sentence, what this page helps you do. Search results show it.

97	Every section is optional except the opening. Order the task sections as a reader needs them.
98	
99	- **Headings** start at `##`, are sentence case, and name the job: "Add a marker", not "Adding".
100	  A feature in `src/data/features.json` with an `anchor` needs a heading that makes that anchor.
101	- **Menus** are bold with `▸`, spelled as the app spells them: **Clip ▸ Split**.
102	- **Keys** use the app's symbols in `<kbd>`: <kbd>⌘T</kbd>. Inside `AtAGlance`, pass the string.
103	- **Controls** are bold where they appear in a step: choose **Save**.
104	- **Links** are root-absolute with a trailing slash: `/timeline/markers/#add-a-marker`. The build
105	  fails on a link or anchor that does not exist.
106	- **Asides** are for what a reader must not miss, not for decoration: `:::note`, `:::tip`,
107	  `:::caution`, `:::danger`.
108	- **Screens** come from `src/assets/screens/`. A `name` is the file name without its look and
109	  extension. Use a screen only when it shows what the page is about, not when the thing is out
110	  of frame, and give it real alt text.
111	
112	## MDX traps
113	
114	MDX is JSX. In prose, `{`, `}` and `<` start code. Put anything like `{x}`, `<1 s` or `a<b` in a
115	code span, or write it out ("under 1 s"). `<kbd>` and every component must close. A line starting
116	with `import` or `export` is code. Leave a blank line after an opening component tag and before
117	its closing tag, or the Markdown inside won't render.
118	
119	## Checking a page
120	
121	```sh
122	node docs/site/scripts/check-pages.mjs <page.mdx>…        # parses, imports, links, captures
123	python3 tools/proof/docs_site_proof.py --pages <page.mdx>…  # internal words, local paths
124	pnpm build                                                # in docs/site: the last word
125	```

127	## Screens
128	
129	The captures come from the screen catalog (`designs/screens/`, `tools/proof/screens.py`), so the
130	pictures are of the real app. To refresh them:
131	
132	```sh
133	python3 tools/proof/screens.py --out <dir>                      # from the repository root
134	node docs/site/scripts/import-screens.mjs <dir> --used
135	```
136	
137	**This site is public.** `import-screens.mjs` refuses a capture whose layout dump holds a local
138	path, and its `CROP` table is the only way past that, by cutting the region away. Settings needs
139	it: its MCP section prints the helper's full path. Never weaken the refusal.

2	title: "Editing inside a nest"
3	description: "Open a nest with set_scope or name one on a single call with scope, and see what follows the open nest and what won't work inside one."
4	---
5	
6	import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
7	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
8	
9	A [nest](/editing/nests/) is a group of clips collapsed into one clip, and it has its own tracks, clips and clock. An agent can work inside one in two ways: open it, as you would, or name it on a single call.
10	
11	<AtAGlance
12	  menu={['Clip ▸ Open Nest', 'Clip ▸ Close Nest']}
13	  keys={['⌘↓', '⌘↑']}
14	  where="Double-click a nest clip"
15	  tools="set_scope"
16	/>
17	
18	## Choose how to get in
19	
20	| | Open it with `set_scope` | Name it with `scope` |
21	| --- | --- | --- |
22	| What it is | A change of view, like double-clicking the nest clip | An argument on one edit tool |
23	| How long it lasts | Until `set_scope` with no arguments | That one call |
24	| What it reaches | A nest a clip shows, at any depth | Any nest in the project, shown or not |
25	| Who it affects | Every later call, and what the window shows | Only that call. The window stays where it is |
26	| When to use it | You want to look: `get_project`, `render_frame`, or a tool that takes no `scope` | You want one edit, from wherever you are |
27	
28	Editing doesn't need the nest open. Opening it is how you see what an edit did.
29	
30	## Open and close a nest with `set_scope`
31	
32	`set_scope` mirrors double-clicking a nest clip, or **Clip ▸ Open Nest** (<kbd>⌘↓</kbd>). Called with no arguments it comes back out, as **Clip ▸ Close Nest** (<kbd>⌘↑</kbd>) does, but all the way to the timeline in one call.
33	
34	| Argument | Type | Required | What it does |
35	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
36	| `clip` | integer | No | The nest clip to open. Works at any depth, and is the precise choice. |
37	| `nest` | integer | No | The nest to open, by id. A clip on the timeline has to show it. |
38	| `project` | string | No | The path of the open project to act on. Leave it out for the frontmost one. |
39	
40	Give `clip` or `nest`, never both. Giving neither means the timeline.
41	
42	**`clip` is the one to prefer.** Two clips can show one nest, and each measures the times inside from its own start, so only the clip says which of them you mean. It finds the clip in the timeline or in any nest, and the call means the same thing wherever you are now, so there's no need to step down one level at a time.
43	
44	**`nest` looks at the timeline only.** Where two timeline clips show the nest, the earliest is entered, and a tie goes to the lower id. A nest that's shown only from inside another nest can't be reached this way. Name its nest clip with `clip`, or send the edit with `scope`, which needs no view at all.
45	
46	### While a nest is open
47	
48	- [`get_project`](/mcp/get-project/#the-report-while-a-nest-is-open) reports the nest as if it were the project, and [`render_frame`](/mcp/render-frame/) draws it at its own size.
49	- Every edit lands inside the nest, unless the call has a `scope` of its own or is one of the [document edits](#document-edits-while-a-nest-is-open).
50	- The playhead, the selection and the range all belong to the nest. Times you send and read are measured from the nest's own zero.
51	
52	`set_scope` moves the view and edits nothing, so it adds no undo step. The playhead moves with it so the frame under it stays the same, as it does [for you](/editing/inside-a-nest/#where-the-playhead-goes). Every change of nest clears the in and out range. Going in clears the selection, and coming out selects the nest clip you went in through.
53	
54	If an edit or an undo takes away the nest that's open, Frame Job falls back to the nearest level that still exists.
55	
56	### What it answers
57	
58	| Key | What it holds |
59	| --- | --- |
60	| `ok` | `true`. |
61	| `scope` | The open nest's id, the number an edit's `scope` takes. `null` at the timeline. |
62	| `scope_clip` | The nest clip it was entered through. |
63	| `scope_path` | The trail from the timeline, one `{nest, clip, name}` for each level. |
64	| `playhead` | The playhead, in the nest's own time. |
65	| `project` | The project summary. |
66	
67	`scope_clip` and `scope_path` appear only while a nest is open. `get_project` reports the same three keys.
68	
69	### When it refuses
70	
71	| It says | Why |
72	| --- | --- |
73	| "Pass nest or clip, not both…" | Both arguments were given. |
74	| "No clip has id 17, in this timeline or in any of its nests…" | No clip anywhere has that id. |
75	| "Clip 17 does not show a nest, so there is nothing to open inside it…" | The clip exists but isn't a nest clip. Its `source.kind` isn't `nest`. |
76	| "no nest with id 4…" | The project has no such nest. |
77	| "No clip on the timeline shows nest 4, so the view cannot reach it in one step…" | The nest is shown only from inside another nest, or by no clip at all. |
78	
79	## The `scope` argument
80	
81	Every edit tool takes an optional `scope`, a nest id, so one call edits inside that nest from wherever the window is looking. It's the same edit and still one undo step.
82	
83	```json
84	{ "clips": [41], "at": 1200000, "scope": 4 }
85	```
86	
87	Sent to `split`, that cuts clip 41 inside nest 4, at 2 s on the nest's own clock.
88	
89	To find the id, read `nests` in `get_project`, or the `source.project` of the nest clip that shows it.
90	
91	With `scope`:
92	
93	- Every clip, track and action id is looked up in that nest, not on the timeline.
94	- Every time is the nest's own, measured from its zero. A nest has no speed, so a moment on the timeline is that time less the nest clip's start.
95	- Media ids don't change, because a nest shares the project's media.
96	- It outranks any nest that's open. To edit the timeline while a nest is open you can't name the timeline, so call `set_scope` with no arguments first.
97	
98	Leave `scope` out, or send `null`, to edit whatever is open: the timeline, or the nest `set_scope` entered.
99	
100	The answer carries `scope`, the nest the edit landed in, so you can tell it from an edit on the timeline. Clips and tracks the edit made are listed in `new_clips` and `new_tracks` wherever they landed. The `project` summary in the same answer counts the timeline's tracks and clips, so it doesn't move when an edit lands in a nest.
101	
102	### When a `scope` is refused
103	
104	A `scope` is checked before any other argument, because it decides what the rest of the call means.
105	
106	| It says | Why |
107	| --- | --- |
108	| "no nest with id 4. get_project lists them under nests, and a nest clip's source.project names the one it shows." | The project has no such nest. |
109	| "scope must be a nest id, not …" | The value isn't a whole number that could be an id. A negative number, a fraction, a true or false and a number written as a string are all refused. |
110	| "No clip has id 17 inside nest 4…" | The id isn't in that nest. The sentence goes on to say how to get back: drop the `scope`, or, when the nest is only open, call `set_scope` with no arguments. Tracks work the same way. |
111	| "detect_silence does not take scope. It takes …" | The tool isn't an edit tool. See [below](#tools-that-follow-the-open-nest). |
112	
113	## Tools that follow the open nest
114	
115	Tools that aren't plain edits take no `scope`, and refuse one by name. They work in whatever nest `set_scope` has open, and on the timeline otherwise, so open the nest first to measure or place inside it.
116	
117	| What it does | Tools |
118	| --- | --- |
119	| Measure and read | `detect_silence`, `detect_fillers`, `get_timeline_transcript`, `get_media_analysis`, `get_cursor_events` |
120	| Sound | `normalize_clip`, `enhance_voice`, `match_audio`, `sync_audio` |
121	| Captions and words | `transcribe`, `transcribe_for_fillers`, `import_captions`, `export_captions`, `relay_captions` |
122	| Picture and timing | `split_at_shots`, `analyze_cutout`, `auto_zoom`, `add_shortcut_overlays`, `speed_up_typing`, `switch_angle`, `switch_by_speaker` |
123	| Adding things | `insert_graphic`, which places its clip in the nest, and `record_screen`, which does the same |
124	| View state | `set_playhead`, `set_range`, `set_selection` |
125	
126	A tool that takes a while reads the project first and checks it again before it edits. If the project or the open nest changed meanwhile, it stops and changes nothing, and says to call it again.
127	
128	Three tools work on the top-level timeline only. With a nest open they refuse, saying to call `set_scope` with no nest first:
129	
130	- `text_behind_subject`
131	- `new_project_from_range`
132	- `make_vertical_version`
133	
134	`rename_graphic` won't run with a nest open either, because it renames the module for every clip in the project. Call `set_scope` with no arguments, then rename.
135	
136	`export` and `save_project` ignore the open nest. `export` writes from the timeline, never the nest, and `save_project` saves the whole project.
137	
138	## `protected_nests` in `detect_silence`
139	
140	[Remove Silences](/cleanup/remove-silences/) never cuts into a nest, so a quiet stretch that runs across one is left alone. `detect_silence` names those nest clips under `protected_nests`, because there may be dead air inside them.
141	
142	<Steps>
143	
144	1. Call `detect_silence`. Read `protected_nests`, a list of nest clip ids.
145	
146	2. Call `set_scope` with `clip` set to one of those ids.
147	
148	3. Call `detect_silence` again. It now measures inside the nest, and its times are the nest's own.
149	
150	4. Pass the ranges to `ripple_delete_ranges`, which lands in the open nest. Like any edit tool it also takes `scope`.
151	
152	5. Call `set_scope` with no arguments to come back out.
153	
154	</Steps>
155	
156	## What doesn't work inside a nest
157	
158	Some edits are about the whole project, so a nest has nothing for them to change. What happens depends on whether the nest was named with `scope` or is only open.
159	
160	| Edit | With `scope` | With the nest only open |
161	| --- | --- | --- |
162	| `add_marker` | Refused | Refused |
163	| `set_marker` with a `time` | Refused | Refused |
164	| `set_marker` without a `time` | Refused | Lands on the project |
165	| `remove_marker` | Refused | Lands on the project |
166	| `set_canvas` | Refused | Lands on the project |
167	| `add_media`, `relink_media`, `remove_media` | Refused | Land on the project |
168	| `set_media_color`, `set_media_speech`, `set_media_cursor` | Refused | Land on the project |
169	| `add_adjustment_clip` | Refused | Refused |
170	| `set_track` with `compressor` or `limiter` | Refused | Refused |
171	
172	### Edit tools refused with a scope
173	
174	Eleven tools have no meaning inside a nest and refuse a `scope` by name, for example "add_marker has no meaning inside nest 4".
175	
176	| Tools | Why |
177	| --- | --- |
178	| `add_marker`, `set_marker`, `remove_marker` | A nest has no markers. Markers are project time, and they become chapters in the exported file. |
179	| `set_canvas` | The frame rate and background are the project's, and a nest's size was fixed when it was made. |
180	| `add_media`, `relink_media`, `remove_media`, `set_media_color`, `set_media_speech`, `set_media_cursor` | A nest shares the project's one media list. |
181	| `add_adjustment_clip` | An [adjustment clip](/color/adjustment-clips/) grades what's behind it on the timeline only. This one is refused with a nest open too. |
182	
183	`set_track` works inside a nest, except that a track's `compressor` and `limiter` are refused, with or without `scope`: a track's dynamics run on the timeline's own mix. A nest's whole sound goes through the track holding its nest clip, so set them there. Volume, pan and the rest of `set_track` mean the same inside a nest as outside.
184	
185	### Document edits while a nest is open
186	
187	When a nest is only open, and the call has no `scope`, nine of those tools apply to the whole project, because that's what they're about. It's the same as you choosing **File ▸ Add Media…** with a nest open.
188	
189	Those are `set_marker` without a `time`, `remove_marker`, `set_canvas`, `add_media`, `relink_media`, `remove_media`, `set_media_color`, `set_media_speech` and `set_media_cursor`.
190	
191	The answer lists what went to the project under `document_ops`, and leaves `scope` out because nothing landed in the nest:
192	
193	```json
194	{ "ok": true, "document_ops": ["set_canvas"], "project": { … } }
195	```
196	
197	`import_media` adds to the project in the same way, with a nest open or not. It has its own answer, with no `document_ops`.
198	
199	### Markers refused while a nest is open
200	
201	`add_marker`, and `set_marker` with a `time`, are refused while a nest is open, whatever time you send. A marker sits at project time, and every tick in the call is measured from the nest's own zero, so the marker would land somewhere else on the timeline. It's the reason **Mark ▸ Add Marker** is greyed out in there.
202	
203	Leave the nest with `set_scope` and no arguments, then send the time in project ticks. A marker's name, chapter setting and colour mean the same in either place, so `set_marker` still changes those. See [Markers](/timeline/markers/#good-to-know).
204	
205	### Document-wide limits inside a nest
206	
207	An edit can be valid inside the nest and still be refused for the project's sake, because these limits count every nest and the timeline together:
208	
209	| Limit | Counted over |
210	| --- | --- |
211	| 4,096 clips | The timeline and every nest |
212	| 64 tracks | The timeline and every nest |
213	| 8 levels of nesting | The deepest chain of nests |
214	
215	So read the answer rather than assuming the edit landed. A refusal names the limit, for example "too many tracks: 65 (max 64)".
216

2	title: "A typical session"
3	description: "The order an agent works in, from opening a project through placing, changing and checking clips to saving and exporting."
4	---
5	
6	import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
7	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
8	
9	An agent works in Frame Job the way you do: bring the media in, place it, change it, look at the result, then save and export. What's different is that it can't see the window, so it reads the project for the ids it needs and renders a frame to check each step.
10	
11	<AtAGlance
12	  tools={['new_project', 'open_project', 'get_project', 'import_media', 'add_clip', 'render_frame', 'save_project', 'export', 'export_status']}
13	/>
14	
15	## Work through a session
16	
17	<Steps>
18	
19	1. **Open.** Call `open_project` with a path, or `new_project` for a blank 1920 × 1080, 30 fps project with one track. See [Tools: projects and history](/mcp/tools-projects/).
20	
21	2. **Read.** Call `get_project`. It answers the canvas, the playhead and every id. Every other tool names things by those ids.
22	
23	3. **Import.** Call `import_media` with the file's path. It answers the new `media` id and what the file holds: its kind, duration, size, frame rate, and whether it has video, sound or transparency. The file is in the project now, but not on the timeline.
24	
25	4. **Place.** Call `add_clip` with `track`, `media` and `at`. The answer lists the new clip's id under `new_clips`.
26	
27	5. **Change.** Use the edit tools. Each call is one undo step. See [All tools](/mcp/tools/).
28	
29	6. **Check.** Call `render_frame` at the moment that matters, and look at the picture. Do this before and after an edit.
30	
31	7. **Save.** Call `save_project`, with a `path` the first time. It answers once the package is really on disk.
32	
33	8. **Export.** Call `export` with a `preset` and a `path`. It answers at once with an `export_id`. Then call `export_status` until `status` is `done`, `failed` or `cancelled`.
34	
35	</Steps>
36	
37	Steps 5 and 6 are the loop. An edit that comes back `ok` says the project changed, and only a frame says it looks right. If it doesn't, `undo` takes the last step back.
38	
39	## See one from start to finish
40	
41	Here's a short session, each call with its arguments. Times are in ticks, 600,000 to the second, so `1200000` is 2 s.
42	
43	```text
44	new_project   { "path": "~/Movies/Talk.framejob" }
45	get_project   { }
46	import_media  { "path": "~/Movies/talk.mov" }
47	add_clip      { "track": 1, "media": 2, "at": 0 }
48	split         { "clips": [3], "at": 1200000 }
49	render_frame  { "t": 1200000, "max_width": 960 }
50	save_project  { }
51	export        { "preset": "h264", "path": "~/Movies/Talk.mp4" }
52	export_status { "export_id": 1 }
53	```
54	
55	`media` and `clips` here stand for the ids the earlier answers gave. Read them from each answer rather than guessing, because ids come from one number series that clips, tracks, markers and media all share. See [Units and ids](/mcp/units-and-ids/).
56	
57	`save_project` needs no `path` here because `new_project` was given one. A project made without one stays an untitled draft until the first `save_project` that names a path.
58	
59	## Follow the export
60	
61	`export` puts the job on the [Export Queue](/export/export-queue/) and returns. It doesn't wait for the file.
62	
63	`export_status` never waits either, so pause between calls. While the job runs, its answer has `progress`, from 0 to 1. When `status` is `done`, the answer says what the file holds, including its size in `bytes`, its settings and its loudness. `failed` and `cancelled` come with a `reason`.
64	
65	To stop a job, call `cancel_export`. See [Export: start, then poll](/mcp/export/).
66	
67	## Good to know
68	
69	- Tools act on the frontmost project. With more than one open, pass `project`, the path `get_project` reports. See [How tool calls behave](/mcp/tool-calls/).
70	- A call that can't do what it's asked comes back with the reason, and the project stays as it was. See [What a call answers](/mcp/what-a-call-answers/).
71	- `render_frame` and `export` differ inside a [nest](/mcp/nests/). With a nest open, `render_frame` draws the nest, but `export` still writes from the timeline.
72	- `export` replaces a file already at the path, and adds the container's extension when the path has none.
73	- `unsaved_changes` in `get_project` says whether there's anything still to save.
74

2	title: "Read the project: get_project"
3	description: "What get_project answers: the project's contents and ids, the playhead and selection, its graphics, a file's Camera Log, and the report while a nest is open."
4	---
5	
6	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
7	
8	`get_project` answers the whole project as JSON, the same document every edit changes. Read it first, because every other tool names things by the ids it reports.
9	
10	<AtAGlance tools="get_project" />
11	
12	## Read the project
13	
14	The only argument is `project`, the path of the open project to read. Leave it out for the frontmost one. The call changes nothing.
15	
16	Three things hold for everything it answers:
17	
18	- Times are ticks, 600,000 to the second.
19	- Clip, track, marker and media ids share one number series, so an id means one thing on its own.
20	- `tracks[0]` is the back of the layer stack, the bottom lane of the timeline.
21	
22	See [Units and ids](/mcp/units-and-ids/).
23	
24	## What it answers
25	
26	| Key | What it holds |
27	| --- | --- |
28	| `project` | The project itself. See [below](#what-project-holds). |
29	| `path` | Where the project is saved. Before its first save, a project opened from a movie, sound file or picture reports that file, and any other project reports `null`. |
30	| `name` | The project's name, as its window shows it. |
31	| `unsaved_changes` | `true` when there's something to save. |
32	| `duration` | The timeline's length in ticks. |
33	| `playhead` | The playhead, in ticks. |
34	| `selection` | The ids of the selected clips, lowest first. |
35	| `in_out_range` | `start` and `end` in ticks. Only there when a range is set. |
36	| `scope` | The id of the [open nest](#the-report-while-a-nest-is-open), or `null` at the timeline. |
37	| `missing_media` | The ids of media whose file has moved. Only there when one has. `relink_media` points one at its new place. |
38	| `graphics` | The project's [graphic modules](#the-graphics-summary). |
39	| `note` | A reminder of the rules above. With a nest open, it also says what's different. |
40	
41	`playhead`, `selection` and `in_out_range` are the app's own state. They aren't saved with the project, and setting them isn't an undo step.
42	
43	## What `project` holds
44	
45	| Key | What it holds |
46	| --- | --- |
47	| `canvas` | The picture's settings. See the next table. |
48	| `media` | Every file in the project, whether or not a clip uses it. |
49	| `tracks` | The timeline's tracks, back to front. |
50	| `clips` | The timeline's clips. |
51	| `markers` | The timeline's markers. |
52	| `nests` | Every nest, each with its own `id`, `name`, `width`, `height`, `tracks` and `clips`. |
53	| `next_id` | The id the next new thing will take. |
54	| `version` | The project file's version. |
55	
56	| `canvas` key | What it holds |
57	| --- | --- |
58	| `width`, `height` | The canvas size in pixels. |
59	| `fps` | The frame rate as `[num, den]`, so 29.97 fps is `[30000, 1001]`. |
60	| `background` | The canvas background. |
61	| `fit_new_clips` | Whether a new clip is scaled to fit when its source is bigger than the canvas. |
62	| `timecode_frames` | Whether timecode reads `HH:MM:SS:FF` rather than `HH:MM:SS.mmm`. |
63	| `output` | `hlg` in an [HDR project](/hdr/dynamic-range/). Left out in an SDR project. |
64	| `blending` | `linear` with [linear-light blending](/hdr/blending/) on. Left out otherwise. |
65	
66	A media entry has `id`, `path`, `kind`, `duration`, `width`, `height`, `fps`, `has_video`, `has_audio` and `has_alpha`, and sometimes more: `original` for a copy, `color` for [its colour setting](#camera-log-readback), `speech` for saved speech spans and `cursor` for a recording's cursor file.
67	
68	A clip has `id`, `track`, `start`, `duration`, `source`, `enabled`, `speed` and `actions`. What it shows sits in `video`, `audio`, `text`, `shape` or `graphic`. `source.kind` says what kind of clip it is, and a nest clip's `source.project` is the id of the nest it shows.
69	
70	## The graphics summary
71	
72	`graphics` is a list with one entry for each module in the project's graphics folder, in name order:
73	
74	| Key | What it holds |
75	| --- | --- |
76	| `name` | The module's name. |
77	| `revision` | The module's revision. It changes when the text does. |
78	| `ok` | `true` when the module compiles. |
79	| `clips` | The ids of the clips drawn by it, on the timeline and in every nest. |
80	
81	`ok: false` means the module doesn't compile. Fix it before exporting, because `export` won't start while a graphic clip's module doesn't compile. See [Graphics with an agent](/graphics/agents-and-graphics/).
82	
83	The list is empty in a project with no modules, and in a project that has no window.
84	
85	## Camera Log readback
86	
87	A file's colour setting is in `color` on its media entry. A file with no setting has no `color`, and each key below appears only when it's set.
88	
89	| Key | What it holds |
90	| --- | --- |
91	| `log` | The curve: `apple_log`, `apple_log2`, `slog3`, `vlog`, `canon_log2` or `canon_log3`. |
92	| `gamut` | The gamut: `bt2020`, `apple_wide_gamut`, `s_gamut3_cine`, `s_gamut3`, `v_gamut` or `cinema_gamut`. |
93	| `lut` | The media id of a [LUT](/hdr/log-luts/) used as the conversion, in place of `log`. |
94	| `detected` | `true` when Frame Job read the setting from the file at import. |
95	| `pq` | An HDR10 file's peak: `file` is what import read, in cd/m², `from` is where it read it (`max_cll` or `mastering_display`), and `peak` is an override. An empty `pq` still marks the file as HDR10. |
96	
97	`detected: true` is how to tell a setting the file declared from one a person or an agent chose. Setting the Camera Log with `set_media_color` replaces it and drops `detected`. See [Camera Log](/hdr/camera-log/).
98	
99	## The report while a nest is open
100	
101	While `set_scope` has a nest open, `get_project` reports the nest as if it were the project, so the ids you read are the ones the next edit can name.
102	
103	- `project.tracks` and `project.clips` are the nest's own.
104	- `project.canvas` has the nest's fixed size. Its other settings are the project's.
105	- `project.markers` is empty, because a nest has no markers.
106	- `project.media` and `project.nests` are still the whole project's, but the open nest's own row under `nests` has no tracks or clips, because they're at the top level here.
107	- `duration`, `playhead`, `selection` and `in_out_range` are the nest's, measured from its own zero.
108	
109	Two more keys say where you are:
110	
111	| Key | What it holds |
112	| --- | --- |
113	| `scope_clip` | The nest clip it was entered through. |
114	| `scope_path` | The trail of nests from the timeline, one `{nest, clip, name}` for each level. |
115	
116	`scope` is the nest's id, the same number an edit's `scope` argument takes. At the timeline `scope` is `null`, and the two keys above aren't there.
117	
118	`render_frame` follows the same view and draws the nest at its own size. Opening a nest is a change of view, not an undo step. See [Editing inside a nest](/mcp/nests/).
119

2	title: "Check the picture: render_frame"
3	description: "Render one frame of the finished timeline so an agent can see its work, choose the file it writes, draw grade and HDR variants, and measure the scopes."
4	---
5	
6	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
7	
8	`render_frame` draws one frame of the finished timeline, so an agent can see what it has done. It goes through the same composition and compositor an export uses, so the picture is what the file will contain at that moment, not a preview of it.
9	
10	<AtAGlance
11	  menu="File ▸ Save Frame…"
12	  keys="⌥⌘E"
13	  tools="render_frame"
14	/>
15	
16	## Render a frame
17	
18	With no arguments it draws the frame under the playhead at the canvas's size and writes a PNG to a temporary file.
19	
20	```json
21	{ "t": 1200000, "path": "/tmp/shot.png", "max_width": 960 }
22	```
23	
24	The picture comes back two ways: as an image the model can see, and as a file on disk. The text beside it says what was drawn and ends by naming the file:
25	
26	```
27	Frame at 1200000 ticks of a 1920×1080 px canvas, rendered at 960×540 px. Written to /tmp/shot.png.
28	```
29	
30	It uses the same writer as [**File ▸ Save Frame…**](/export/save-frame/), so a PNG from either one is identical, byte for byte.
31	
32	With a [nest](/mcp/nests/) open, it draws that nest at its own size, from its own zero, without the nest clip's position, scale or opacity. It takes no `scope`, so open the nest with `set_scope` to look inside.
33	
34	| Argument | Type | Required | What it does | Default |
35	| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
36	| [`t`](#t) | integer | No | The moment to render, in ticks. | The playhead |
37	| [`path`](#path) | string | No | Where to write the file. | A temporary file |
38	| [`format`](#format) | string | No | `png`, `jpeg` or `heic`. | From the path, else `png` |
39	| [`max_width`](#max_width) | integer | No | Caps the width in pixels, 16 to 8192. | The canvas's width |
40	| [`burn_in_timecode`](#burn_in_timecode) | boolean | No | Draws the project timecode over the picture. | `false` |
41	| [`ungraded`](#ungraded) | boolean | No | Draws every clip as if it weren't graded. | `false` |
42	| [`selection`](#selection) | integer | No | Draws what an adjustment clip's qualifier selects. | None |
43	| [`sdr_version`](#sdr_version) | boolean | No | Draws an HDR project's SDR version. | `false` |
44	| [`waveform`](#waveform-parade-and-histogram) | boolean | No | Also measures the waveform. | `false` |
45	| [`parade`](#waveform-parade-and-histogram) | boolean | No | Also measures the RGB parade. | `false` |
46	| [`histogram`](#waveform-parade-and-histogram) | boolean | No | Also measures the histogram. | `false` |
47	| [`vectorscope`](#vectorscope-and-vectorscope_zoom) | boolean | No | Also measures the vectorscope. | `false` |
48	| [`vectorscope_zoom`](#vectorscope-and-vectorscope_zoom) | integer | No | 1, 2 or 4. Needs `vectorscope`. | 1 |
49	| `project` | string | No | The path of the open project to act on. | The frontmost project |
50	
51	## Choose the moment and the file
52	
53	### `t`
54	
55	The moment to render, in ticks, 600,000 to the second. It's rounded to the project's frame grid. Leave it out for the playhead. A time before zero draws the first frame, and a time past the end is refused.
56	
57	With a nest open, `t` and the playhead are the nest's own time.
58	
59	### `path`
60	
61	Where to write the file, for example `~/Desktop/shot.png`. The folder must already exist, because Frame Job won't create one. An empty `path` is refused.
62	
63	Leave it out for a temporary file. Either way, the last sentence of the text names the file written.
64	
65	### `format`
66	
67	The kind of file to write.
68	
69	| `format` | What you get |
70	| --- | --- |
71	| `png` | Lossless, keeping the canvas's transparency. |
72	| `jpeg` | Quality 0.9. JPEG has no transparency, so a transparent canvas is flattened onto black, and the text always says so. |
73	| `heic` | Quality 0.9, keeping the canvas's transparency. |
74	
75	With no `format`, the path's extension decides: `.jpg` and `.jpeg` both mean JPEG, and `.heic` means HEIC. Any other path writes a PNG.
76	
77	An explicit `format` wins, and the path's extension is replaced rather than added to, so `{"path": "shot.jpg", "format": "png"}` writes `shot.png`. Only an extension Frame Job knows is replaced: `Talk v1.2` becomes `Talk v1.2.png`, not `Talk v1.png`. A JPEG always ends `.jpg`, so `shot.jpeg` is written as `shot.jpg`.
78	
79	`jpg` also works as a `format`, and capitals don't matter.
80	
81	### `max_width`
82	
83	Caps the image's width in pixels, from 16 to 8192. The picture keeps its shape and is never made larger than the canvas. Leave it out for the canvas's own size.
84	
85	A smaller frame is quicker to send and to look at. The [scopes](#measure-the-frame) measure the frame as written, so their counts cover fewer pixels too.
86	
87	## Change what's drawn
88	
89	These four draw something other than the plain picture. The view switches in the window never reach this tool or an export, so an agent asks here.
90	
91	### `burn_in_timecode`
92	
93	Draws the project timecode over the picture, on top of everything, as the export sheet's **Burn in timecode** does. It's the project's own timecode, in the toolbar's spelling. See [Burn in timecode](/export/burn-in-timecode/).
94	
95	### `ungraded`
96	
97	Draws every clip as if it weren't graded: Light, Color, wheels and curves neutral, and no look. It's the picture **View ▸ Show Ungraded** gives. See [Show Ungraded](/color/show-ungraded/).
98	
99	### `selection`
100	
101	Takes an adjustment clip's id and draws what its qualifier selects, in place of grading. It's the picture **View ▸ Show Selection** gives.
102	
103	- White is fully graded, and black is untouched.
104	- It's the blurred selection when the qualifier has a blur, and it's multiplied by any matte cutting the clip.
105	- The clip's strength isn't applied.
106	- Every layer in front of the clip is left out.
107	- Where the clip isn't on the frame, the picture is black.
108	
109	Frame Job won't do this for any other kind of clip. See [Qualifiers](/color/qualifiers/).
110	
111	### `sdr_version`
112	
113	Draws an [HDR project's](/hdr/dynamic-range/) SDR version, the picture **View ▸ Show SDR Version** gives. White titles come back near white, and highlights above reference white roll off. It's what the SDR exports and JPEG frames hold.
114	
115	In an SDR project it changes nothing, and the frame comes out identical. See [Show SDR Version](/hdr/show-sdr-version/).
116	
117	## Measure the frame
118	
119	Each scope argument measures the rendered frame through the same analyser as the [**View ▸ Scopes**](/color/scopes/) panel, so the two can't count differently. The text gives the headline figures, and a JSON file beside the image holds the counts, named after it: `shot.png` gets `shot.png.waveform.json`.
120	
121	The scopes read the frame as it was drawn, so `max_width`, `burn_in_timecode`, `ungraded` and `selection` all change what they count.
122	
123	If the measurement can't run, the call comes back as an error, but the image is already written and the error names it: "Wrote …, but its waveform could not be measured: the GPU pass did not run."
124	
125	### `waveform`, `parade` and `histogram`
126	
127	- **`waveform`** measures luma. The text gives the share of pixels clipping high and low.
128	- **`parade`** measures R′, G′ and B′ the way the waveform measures luma. The text gives the share clipping high and low for each channel.
129	- **`histogram`** counts R′, G′, B′ and Y′ at 256 levels. The text gives the share clipping high and low, read from Y′.
130	
131	For example: "Waveform: highlights clipped in 0.4 % of pixels, shadows in 0.0 %; its 256 × 256 counts are in …". A pixel clips high at level 255 and low at level 0.
132	
133	| JSON key | `waveform` | `parade` | `histogram` |
134	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
135	| `width`, `height` | The frame measured | The frame measured | The frame measured |
136	| `levels` | 256 | 256 | 256 |
137	| `columns` | 256 | 256 | |
138	| `counts` | 256 column bins, each 256 levels | The same, under `red`, `green` and `blue` | |
139	| `red`, `green`, `blue`, `luma` | | | 256 counts each |
140	| `clipped_high`, `clipped_low` | Pixels clipping | Pixels clipping, by channel | Pixels clipping, by Y′ |
141	| `marks_high`, `marks_low` | The column bins where at least 0.5 % of the column clips | The same, by channel | |
142	| `highlights`, `shadows` | Percentages | | Percentages |
143	
144	### `vectorscope` and `vectorscope_zoom`
145	
146	`vectorscope` measures Rec. 709 Cb and Cr of the encoded values in 256 × 256 bins centred on neutral, bin 128. The text gives the share of pixels that are neutral.
147	
148	`vectorscope_zoom` is 1, 2 or 4, like the 1×, 2× and 4× cells on a [vectorscope](/color/vectorscope/) slot, and it needs `vectorscope: true`. Zooming spreads a near-grey picture over more bins. At 2 and 4, a pixel off the plot isn't counted, and the text also gives the share that lie off it.
149	
150	| JSON key | What it holds |
151	| --- | --- |
152	| `width`, `height` | The frame measured. |
153	| `bins`, `centre` | 256 and 128. |
154	| `matrix`, `values` | `Rec. 709` and `encoded`. |
155	| `counts` | 256 arrays by Cr bin, each indexed by Cb bin. |
156	| `neutral` | Pixels in the neutral bin. |
157	| `zoom` | The zoom. |
158	| `off_plot` | Pixels left off the plot. Always 0 at 1. |
159	| `targets` | The six 75 % colour targets, `R`, `Mg`, `B`, `Cy`, `G` and `Yl`, each `[cb, cr]` in bins at this zoom, or `null` off the plot. |
160	| `skin_line_degrees` | The skin line's angle. |
161	
162	## Read what the answer says
163	
164	The text always starts with the frame's time and sizes and ends with "Written to …". Anything else worth saying sits between the two.
165	
166	### Graphic problems in the answer
167	
168	When a [graphic](/graphics/agents-and-graphics/) in the frame had a problem, the answer names it with its frame and the diagnostic:
169	
170	- `Graphic "lower-third" failed at frame 12: …`
171	- `Graphic "lower-third" warned at frame 12: …`
172	- `Graphic "lower-third" does not compile: …`
173	
174	A failed graphic draws its error card in the picture.
175	
176	### Waiting for cutout masks
177	
178	A clip with [Remove Background](/effects/remove-background/) waits up to 30 s for the masks the frame needs. Frame Job starts making them as soon as the cutout is set, on your Mac.
179	
180	Past 30 s the clip is drawn whole, and the answer says so: "Clip 12 is drawn uncut: its person masks were not ready within 30 s." For a picture with its subject set to foreground, it says "its foreground masks".
181	
182	So after setting a cutout, read that sentence before trusting the frame. [`analyze_cutout`](/mcp/tools-analysis/) can wait for the masks first.
183	
184	### A cursor that can't be drawn
185	
186	A screen recording's cursor is drawn from its cursor file. When the file can't be read, the clip draws without one and the answer says "The cursor of media 5 is not drawn: …".
187	
188	## Frames from an HDR project
189	
190	In an [HLG project](/hdr/dynamic-range/), the frame depends on the format:
191	
192	| What you ask for | What you get |
193	| --- | --- |
194	| `png` | 16-bit, labelled BT.2100 HLG |
195	| `heic` | 10-bit, labelled BT.2100 HLG |
196	| `jpeg` | The project's SDR version, labelled BT.709 |
197	| Any format with `sdr_version` | The project's SDR version, labelled BT.709 |
198	
199	Scopes read the picture drawn. On the HLG picture they read the HLG signal, and on the SDR version they read as an SDR project's do.
200	
201	On the HLG signal:
202	
203	- Each scope's JSON adds `signal: "hlg"`.
204	- The waveform, parade and histogram JSON add `scale`: `unit` (`cd/m²`), `ticks` (each with `percent`, `level` and `nits`), `reference_white_percent` (75) and `clip_percent` (100).
205	- Luma takes Rec. 2020's weights, and the vectorscope takes Rec. 2020's matrix and targets.
206	- The text says so. The waveform's reads "reference white at 75 %, 203 cd/m², and 100 % at 1,000 cd/m²".
207	
208	See [Scopes in an HDR project](/hdr/hdr-scopes/) and [Export HDR](/hdr/export-hdr/).
209	
210	## When it won't render
211	
212	Nothing is drawn in these cases, and the answer says why.
213	
214	| It says | What to do |
215	| --- | --- |
216	| "No frame at … Either the time is past the end of the timeline, the media is missing, or the timeline is empty." | Check `duration` and `missing_media` in [`get_project`](/mcp/get-project/). |
217	| "There is no folder at … to write into." | Create the folder, or choose another `path`. |
218	| "path must name a file to write — omit it for a temporary one." | The `path` was empty. |
219	| "format must be one of png, jpeg, heic (got …)." | Use one of the three. |
220	| "max_width must be 16…8192 px (got …)." | Use a width in range. |
221	| "selection must name an adjustment clip of this project; clip … is not one." | Pass an adjustment clip's id. An adjustment clip can't be inside a nest, so close any open nest first. |
222	| "vectorscope_zoom must be 1, 2 or 4 (got …)." | Use one of the three. |
223	| "vectorscope_zoom needs vectorscope: true." | Add `vectorscope: true`. |
